concepts.learning_objective: Distinguish naturally occurring magnets (lodestones) from the artificial magnets used in everyday objects.
Classify materials as magnetic or non-magnetic and name iron, nickel and cobalt as magnetic metals.
Identify the poles as the parts of a magnet where its attraction is strongest.
Explain that North and South poles always occur in pairs, whatever the size or shape of the magnet.
Explain that a freely suspended magnet rests along the north-south direction and use this to tell a magnet from an iron bar.
Describe the parts of a magnetic compass and how it is used to find directions.

topics.title: Making a magnet and a compass

concepts.learning_objective: Describe how an iron needle is made into a magnet by stroking it with one pole of a magnet and how to test it.
Explain how a magnetised needle on a floating cork, or the matsya-yantra, works as a compass.
State that unlike poles attract and like poles repel, and apply this to magnets and compass needles.
Use repulsion to tell a magnet from a piece of iron.
Recognise that the magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials such as wood, cardboard, plastic and glass.

topics.title: Fun with magnets and caring for magnets

concepts.learning_objective: Apply the properties of magnets to solve everyday problems and explain magnet-based toys.
State how magnets should be stored and handled so that they stay strong.
